title: Simple Liquid Treatment Stops Tooth Decay in Children Without Drilling, Major Trial Finds
excerpt: A University of Michigan-led clinical trial shows silver diamine fluoride painted onto cavities can halt decay in seconds, offering a painless alternative for young children.
body:
• Silver diamine fluoride (SDF) stopped tooth decay in more than half of affected baby teeth when applied every six months
  • The Phase III trial, published in JAMA Pediatrics, enrolled 830 children under age 6 across Michigan, New York and Iowa
  • The treatment takes only seconds per tooth, requires no drilling, injections or sedation
  • SDF could pave the way for FDA approval as a cavity treatment, potentially transforming paediatric dental care

A cheap, painless liquid that can be painted onto a child's tooth in seconds has been shown to halt cavity progression without drilling or sedation, according to the largest U.S. clinical trial of its kind.

The Phase III study, led by the University of Michigan and published in JAMA Pediatrics, found that silver diamine fluoride (SDF) arrested tooth decay in more than half of children's affected baby teeth when applied at six-month intervals.

How It Works

SDF is a clear liquid containing silver and fluoride. Applied to a cavity with a tiny sponge-tipped applicator, the silver kills cavity-causing bacteria and helps stop further destruction of the tooth, while the fluoride helps rebuild and strengthen the enamel. The entire procedure takes just seconds per tooth.

"This is a very effective and safe treatment — even in children as young as 1."

— Margherita Fontana, Professor of Dentistry, University of Michigan

Unlike conventional cavity treatment, which requires removing decayed tooth material with a drill before placing a filling, SDF simply arrests the decay in place. The treatment requires no local anaesthetic, no sedation and no special equipment beyond the applicator.

The Scale of the Problem

Tooth decay is the most common chronic disease of childhood, affecting more than 40% of U.S. children. Untreated cavities send thousands of young children to emergency departments each year for dental problems that hospital doctors typically cannot repair. Many eventually require surgery under general anaesthesia — a procedure that carries its own risks for developing brains.

"Current treatments for severe early childhood caries rely on restoration and tooth extraction, which can involve general anaesthesia. These interventions are expensive, cavities often return, and anaesthesia can have long-term effects on a developing brain. We didn't really have any other options until recently — SDF is a game changer."

— Margherita Fontana

A Long-Used Treatment Gets U.S. Evidence

SDF has been used successfully for decades in countries across Asia, South America and Oceania. In the United States, it was approved as a medical device in 2014 for treating tooth sensitivity, and dentists have since used it off-label for cavities.

However, it lacked the large-scale U.S. clinical evidence typically required for FDA approval as a drug to treat tooth decay. The Michigan-led trial, conducted in collaboration with New York University College of Dentistry and the University of Iowa, provides exactly that evidence.

The study enrolled 830 children under age 6, recruited through dental offices, paediatric practices and Head Start programs in Michigan, New York and Iowa. The trial launched in 2018 and continued through the disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Limitations and Next Steps

SDF is not suitable for all cavities. Teeth with active infection, pain or swelling require more intensive treatment. The treatment also leaves a dark stain on the treated area, which can be cosmetically noticeable on front teeth. However, since it is primarily used on baby teeth that will eventually fall out, the staining is generally considered an acceptable trade-off.

The American Academy of Pediatrics already provides guidance on SDF use in primary care settings, noting it is especially helpful for very young children, those with dental anxiety and children with special healthcare needs.

With the clinical evidence now in hand, the path toward FDA approval as a formal cavity treatment appears significantly clearer. If approved, SDF could transform paediatric dental care by making effective treatment accessible in settings far beyond the traditional dental office.
